Hudsonian godwits undertake one of the most remarkable migrations in the avian world, traveling annually between breeding grounds in the subarctic and wintering areas in southern South America. During these journeys, individuals may cover distances exceeding 15,000 kilometers, relying on strategically located stopover sites to replenish depleted fat reserves. The species exhibits strong site fidelity to both breeding and wintering areas, a trait that facilitates pair formation and resource acquisition within familiar territories. Predation pressure during the nesting period is substantial, with arctic foxes and parasitic jaegers representing significant threats to eggs and chicks. Conservation concerns center on habitat loss at key staging sites, particularly along the coasts of the Great Plains and in the pampas of Argentina, where agricultural intensification and wetland drainage continue to reduce available foraging habitat. Climate change poses an additional long-term risk, as warming temperatures in the Arctic may disrupt the phenological synchrony between hatching dates and the emergence of insect prey, potentially reducing chick survival and overall recruitment into the breeding population.
